label: The Problem of Evil
framing: If God is good and able, why is there so much that is neither. Scripture does not hand the sufferer a tidy answer to that question. It hands them a God who entered the wound rather than explaining it away.
cultural: Our age treats suffering as the strongest case against God, and it is an old case, not a modern one. The ancient world had its own version, the gods were arbitrary and you appeased them. The Bible refuses both the cruel gods and the cheap comfort, letting Job rage for forty chapters and never once rebuking him for the questions, only for assuming he could see the whole.
historical: Augustine in the fourth century argued that evil is not a thing God made but a privation, a good twisted and emptied, and the church largely followed him. The Enlightenment sharpened the problem, with David Hume around 1779 stating the dilemma at its hardest, and Dostoevsky in 1880 putting it in the mouth of Ivan Karamazov, who returns his ticket over the suffering of one child. The cross has remained the church's answer that is not an explanation.
application: Resist the urge to defend God with answers that would shame the sufferer, since Job's friends were the ones rebuked. Let lament be a form of faith, bringing the protest to God rather than away from him. Hold the long view, that the God who hung on a cross is not absent from your pain, and the empty tomb is the promise that he means to undo it.

verses.text: Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding.
We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.
‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.”

label: Heaven and Eternity
framing: Heaven in Scripture is less a misty escape from earth than the healing of it. The Christian hope is not disembodied souls on clouds but a new heaven and a new earth, bodies raised, the world remade, and God himself dwelling among his people.
cultural: Much of what people picture as heaven, the harps and the clouds and the endless rest, owes more to medieval art and sentiment than to the Bible. The wider culture often treats the afterlife as a vague continuation of the self, while Scripture speaks of a renewed creation so concrete it has a city, a river, and a table. The hope is not less physical than this life but more.
historical: The early creeds confessed the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting, not the immortality of the soul alone. The medieval imagination, shaped by Dante's vision around 1320, gave heaven its tiered geography, while N.T. Wright in our own time has pressed the church back toward the New Testament's earthier hope, that the dead are with Christ now and await a bodily resurrection in a renewed world.
application: Let the hope of the world to come loosen your grip on this one without making you useless in it, for those who expect a new earth tend to tend this one with more care, not less. Grieve your dead with hope, since in Christ they are not lost but ahead of you. And measure your treasures against a kingdom that does not rust.

verses.text: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.

In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am.
Rather, as it is written: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”
I am torn between the two. I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.
And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.

label: Hell and Judgment
framing: Hell is the hardest doctrine the church holds, and it should never be held lightly or with relish. Scripture presents it not as God's eagerness to punish but as the terrible ratification of a person's refusal of him, the door, as one writer put it, locked from the inside.
cultural: Our age finds the very idea offensive, and the church has too often deserved the offense, wielding hell as a threat and a recruiting tool. Yet the same culture that recoils at judgment longs for justice and rages when the wicked go free. Scripture holds both, that God will not let evil have the last word and that he takes no pleasure in the death of anyone.
historical: The church has never spoken with one voice here. Augustine in the fifth century held the traditional view of eternal conscious punishment, while figures from Origen in the third century to some modern evangelicals have argued for conditional immortality or a wider hope. C.S. Lewis in 1945 portrayed hell as the self curved finally inward, a place its residents prefer to surrender. The creeds affirm that Christ will come to judge, and leave the rest to him.
application: Hold this doctrine with tears, never satisfaction, remembering you were not spared because you deserved it. Let it sober your witness without weaponizing it, since fear is a poor evangelist and love a better one. And let the reality of judgment drive you not to threaten your neighbor but to long for his rescue, and to leave the verdict to the Judge who is also the one who died for him.

verses.text: Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment,

Say to them: ‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live. Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die, O house of Israel?’
And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
God “will repay each one according to his deeds.”

label: The End Times
framing: Scripture promises that the same Jesus who left will return to set the world right, and that this hope should make Christians awake rather than anxious. The point of biblical prophecy is not a timetable to decode but a King to expect, and a life to live worthy of his coming.
cultural: The end times have become an industry, fueling novels, charts, and the recurring panic of date-setters who are always wrong. Scripture cuts against the whole enterprise, since Jesus himself said no one knows the day or the hour. The wider culture has its own apocalypses now, ecological and technological, and the church can witness to a hope that does not depend on us reading the headlines correctly.
historical: Christians have disagreed about the details from the start, and the disagreement is old. The early church expected Christ's near return, Augustine in the fifth century read Revelation largely as symbol, and the detailed dispensational system most associate with the rapture was developed by John Nelson Darby in the nineteenth century and popularized in the twentieth. Across every view, the creeds confess only this, that he will come again to judge the living and the dead.
application: Hold the details with humility and the hope with confidence, refusing both the date-setting that Jesus forbade and the cynicism that stops expecting him at all. Let his coming shape how you live now, watchful and at work, found faithful rather than merely informed. And do not let speculation about the end distract you from the neighbor in front of you.

verses.text: No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
“Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”
For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise.
But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.
He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

label: The Love of God
framing: The love of God in Scripture is not a sentiment but a costly action, measured at the cross. It does not wait for you to clean yourself up. It is the love that comes for the prodigal while he is still a long way off and runs.
cultural: We use the word love so cheaply that it has nearly lost its weight, a feeling that comes and goes with the mood. Scripture means something sturdier, a covenant loyalty, a love that chooses and keeps choosing. And against a culture that ties worth to performance and approval, the gospel says you are loved before you have earned a thing, and could not have earned it anyway.
historical: The church has fought to keep this love from being reduced to mere affection or mere law. Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth century wrote of loving God for his own sake, Martin Luther in the sixteenth century recovered the scandal that God loves the unlovely rather than finding them lovely first, and the hymn writers of every age have returned again and again to a love that, in the words of one, would not let them go.
application: Let yourself be loved before you try to perform, since the gospel order is grace first and obedience after, never the reverse. When you feel furthest off, remember the father ran toward the son before a word of apology was spoken. And let the love you have received become the love you extend, for we love because he first loved us.

verses.text: But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.”

For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

label: God's Sovereignty
framing: Scripture insists that God reigns over all things, and that this is comfort rather than fatalism. He is not a distant clockmaker nor a tyrant pulling strings, but a Father who works all things, even the ones meant for evil, toward good for those who love him.
cultural: Our age prizes control and panics at its loss, and so the claim that God is sovereign cuts two ways, threatening our autonomy and steadying our fear. Beware the bumper-sticker version, everything happens for a reason, which Scripture never quite says and which can crush the grieving. The Bible holds something deeper, that no suffering is wasted in God's hands, which is not the same as saying every suffering is good.
historical: The church has long held divine sovereignty and human responsibility together without fully resolving the tension. Augustine in the fifth century stressed grace and election against Pelagius, the Reformers sharpened it further, and the Synod of Dort in 1619 and the Arminian remonstrants who opposed it drew the lines most Protestants still live within. Across the divide, all confess that God governs and that we are accountable, both at once.
application: Let God's sovereignty be a pillow to rest on, not a problem to solve, especially when life slips your grasp. Do not use it to explain away another's pain, but let it ground your own peace, that you are held by a hand that does not slip. And hold the mystery honestly, that you are genuinely responsible and he is genuinely in control, and you cannot see the whole.

verses.text: And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.
As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.
A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.
I declare the end from the beginning, and ancient times from what is still to come. I say, ‘My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.’
In Him we were also chosen as God’s own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will,

label: Why Follow Jesus
framing: The case for following Jesus rests finally on the kind of person he was and the claims he made, which were not the claims of a mere teacher. He forgave sins he was not wronged by, accepted worship, and said that to see him was to see the Father. You are not left the option of admiring him from a safe distance.
cultural: Our culture is happy to keep Jesus as a wise teacher, a moral example, a gentle face on a coffee mug, anything but Lord. The trouble, as Lewis pressed, is that a merely human teacher who said the things Jesus said would be a lunatic or a liar, not a sage. The skeptic owes the historical figure a more honest reckoning than the harmless version the culture allows.
historical: From the beginning the church confessed that Jesus is Lord, a claim that cost the early Christians their lives in an empire that demanded the title for Caesar. The Council of Nicaea in 325 and Chalcedon in 451 hammered out that he is fully God and fully man, one person, neither half-divine hero nor mere good man. The skeptic Saul of Tarsus became the apostle Paul not by an argument but by an encounter on the Damascus road.
application: Read the Gospels themselves before you accept anyone's summary of them, and meet the figure rather than the caricature. Bring your honest objections, since faith built on evasion will not hold. And reckon with the cost, that following Jesus is not adding a hobby to your life but handing him the keys, which is the only following he ever offered.

verses.text: Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.
Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”
“But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?”

label: The Resurrection
framing: Christianity stands or falls on one event in history, that a crucified man walked out of his tomb. Paul staked the whole faith on it, saying that if Christ has not been raised, the entire thing is a pity and a lie. It is not a symbol of spring. It is a claim about a Sunday morning.
cultural: The modern assumption is that the resurrection is the sort of thing educated people simply cannot believe, a relic of a pre-scientific age. But the first witnesses were not credulous, they knew as well as we do that dead men stay dead, which is exactly why they fled and doubted. The question the skeptic must face is not why ancient people believed easily, but what turned terrified deserters into people who died for the claim.
historical: The earliest creed Paul cites in 1 Corinthians 15, datable to within a few years of the events, lists named eyewitnesses, most still alive to be questioned. The transformation of the disciples, the empty tomb conceded even by their opponents, the conversion of skeptics like James, the Lord's brother, and Paul, and the church's leap to Sunday worship are the data every theory must explain. Scholars such as N.T. Wright have argued the resurrection remains the best account of them.
application: Examine the evidence honestly rather than dismissing it by reflex, since the case is stronger than most assume and worth your attention. If it happened, nothing else stays the same, for the empty tomb is God's verdict on Jesus and his promise over your own grave. And let it ground your hope, that because he lives, death is a defeated enemy and not the end of your story.

verses.text: And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith.

For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.
He is not here; He has risen! Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee:
and who through the Spirit of holiness was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord.
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.
